questions.prompt: The booking conditions of an agency read: "A deposit of 20 % is payable on booking. The deposit is not refundable less than thirty days before departure." Karim booked in June, paid the deposit, then cancelled ten days before his flight. What happens to his deposit?

options.text: he gets it back in full, since he cancelled
it is turned into a discount on his next booking
he owes the balance of the price as well
he loses it: the agency is entitled to keep it

questions.explanation: The small print says two things and both of them bite here. A deposit is payable on booking, and it stops being refundable once the deadline printed in the conditions has passed. Karim cancelled ten days before departure, well inside the thirty-day limit, so the agency keeps the money. Getting it back in full is what would have happened before that date; a deposit is not converted into a discount on a future trip, which would be a favour and not a right; and a cancelled booking leaves no balance to pay.

questions.prompt: A guest writes to the hotel: "You said that we will be met at the airport, but nobody was there." One word in her report has been left as it was spoken. Which one?

options.text: will
said
met
was

questions.explanation: After a reporting verb in the past, will steps back to would: you said that we would be met at the airport. Will belongs to the moment when the promise was made, in front of a customer who had not travelled yet, and leaving it standing in the report is the commonest mistake of the whole lesson. The reporting verb is already in the past, the past participle inside the passive never moves, and the last verb is the guest's own account of what really happened.

questions.prompt: A customer is complaining at the agency desk. Match each of her sentences with the move it makes in her complaint.

options.text: I'm afraid I have to make a complaint about last week's trip.
Our room had no balcony and looked onto the kitchens.
Your brochure promised a balcony over the gardens.
I'd like the difference between the two rooms refunded.
recalling the promise that was broken
opening the complaint and naming its subject
saying what she wants from the agency
stating what actually happened in the room

questions.explanation: A complaint that works makes four moves in this order. You open it by announcing that it is a complaint and naming its subject, so that nobody has to guess why you are there. You state the facts, plainly, so that nobody has to take your word for them. You recall the promise that was broken, and that is exactly where reported speech is needed, since you are repeating the agency's own words back to it. And you finish by asking for something precise — here the difference between the room she paid for and the room she was given, not the price of the whole holiday.

questions.prompt: You are at the hotel desk. Your room had no hot water for three nights and you want the manager to act. Which sentence complains firmly but politely?

options.text: Your hotel is a disgrace, and the staff at the desk knew it perfectly well.
Sorry to bother you — it doesn't really matter, but the water was cold.
I'd like to make a complaint: we had no hot water for three nights.
Am I supposed to believe that hot water is an extra in your hotel?

questions.explanation: A firm complaint attacks the problem, a rude one attacks the person. Announcing the complaint and naming the fault with its duration keeps the conversation where you need it, on the hot water. Calling the hotel a disgrace and accusing the staff of knowing invites the manager to answer your tone rather than your problem. Saying that it does not really matter is an invitation to do nothing about it. And a sarcastic question about what counts as an extra is an attack wearing the mask of a question.

questions.prompt: Say the word "disappointed" aloud. Which line shows where its main stress falls?

options.text: DIS-ap-point-ed
dis-ap-POINT-ed
dis-AP-point-ed
dis-ap-point-ED

questions.explanation: Disappointed has four syllables and the third is the one said louder, longer and higher: dis-ap-POINT-ed. It is the syllable that carries the meaning of the word, the one you also hear stressed in appoint. English gives a long word exactly one main stress, never two, and the ending -ed of an adjective is never the syllable that takes it.

questions.prompt: At the counter. Customer: "Are the airport taxes included in that price?" Agent: "They are, madam, but the excursions aren't." The customer books the trip. What will she still have to pay for once she is there?

options.text: the taxes at the airport
the tickets for the flight
the rooms at the hotel
the excursions she goes on

questions.explanation: The agent's answer does two jobs in one line: it confirms one thing and excludes another. The taxes are covered by the price she is about to pay, while the excursions are not, so each of them will be paid for on the spot, on the day she goes on it. What is included is never paid twice, and in a package holiday sold at a single price the flight and the hotel are precisely what that price buys.
